podcast.title: Formalization of Gold Records (1958)
podcast.body: In 1958, the RIAA formalized its award system, announcing that any single or album achieving over one million dollars in sales (not copies) in the United States would be certified as a gold record. This applied specifically to sales within the US. "In 1958, the Recording Industry Association of America decided to formalize everything."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Ongoing History Book of Firsts

podcast.title: Reformalization of Sales Awards (1976)
podcast.body: In 1976, the RIAA reformalized its awards, changing the definition of a gold album to 500,000 copies sold in America. Concurrently, a new Platinum Award was introduced to recognize sales of one million copies in the US. "Awards were based on dollar sales until 1976 when things were reformalized."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Ongoing History Book of Firsts

podcast.title: Introduction of Multi-Platinum and Diamond Awards (1984, 1999)
podcast.body: Due to the increasing volume of record sales, Multi-Platinum awards were introduced in 1984, followed by the Diamond Award in 1999 for sales of 10 million copies. In both instances, there were multiple simultaneous recipients, thus no single "first" awardee for these categories. "Multi-platinum awards were introduced in 1984. And then in 1999, they came up with a diamond award, which meant sales of 10 million copies."

podcast.title: Limewire Copyright Lawsuit (2006-2011)
podcast.body: The Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) initiated legal action against the file-sharing site Limewire and its creator, Martin Gordon, in 2006. In 2010, a judge ruled that Limewire and Gordon had infringed upon millions of copyrights, leading to an immediate shutdown order for the service. In 2011, the RIAA, alongside 13 record companies, filed a staggering lawsuit for $75 trillion US dollars, a figure based on infringements of just 11,000 songs, which at the time exceeded the entire global GDP. Though no one possesses such an amount, Gordon ultimately settled for $105 million. This lawsuit, along with others against file-sharing programs like Grokster ($50 million settlement) and another unnamed service ($100 million settlement), marked a significant effort by the music industry to combat piracy. "The IRA took its first legal action against Limewire. That dragged on until 2010 when a judge found that Limewire and Gordon had, in fact, infringed on millions of copyrights and ordered Limewire to be shut down immediately."
